core.p: **Part (b)**: Ambition is an important theme in Macbeth. Explain the importance of ambition **elsewhere in the play**. In your answer you must consider: how ambition is shown; the effects of ambition. You should refer to the **context** of the play in your answer. (20 marks: AO1 and AO3)

bullets: **Thesis**: ambition is a choice, not a fate; it promises power but produces fear and emptiness; Shakespeare warns his audience against rebellion against divine order.
**P1** (Act 1): the idea of murder is Macbeth’s; ‘vaulting ambition’ is self-aware.
**P2** (Lady Macbeth): ambition as partnership and as rejection of nature; her collapse.
**P3** (Acts 3–4): ambition becomes insecurity and tyranny; Banquo as foil.
**P4** (Act 5): ambition ends in ‘nothing’; Malcolm’s restored order.

essays.q: Explain the importance of ambition elsewhere in Macbeth.
essays.text:
Shakespeare presents ambition not as a destiny forced on Macbeth by the Witches but as a desire he chooses to feed; by tracing it from ‘vaulting ambition’ to ‘nothing’, he warns his Jacobean audience that ambition which overturns God’s chosen order destroys the person who pursues it.

From the beginning, Shakespeare makes clear that the idea of murder comes from Macbeth himself. The Witches only greet him as ‘king hereafter’, yet within moments he confesses in an aside to ‘that suggestion / Whose horrid image doth unfix my hair’. The word ‘murder’ is his. Banquo, who hears a similar prophecy, warns that ‘instruments of darkness tell us truths’ to ‘win us to our harm’, and the contrast establishes that the prophecy is a test rather than a command. By Act 1 Scene 7, Macbeth can name his flaw precisely: he has ‘no spur’ but ‘Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself’. The image of a rider leaping so violently that he falls off the other side shows that he understands where ambition will lead. For an audience who had just lived through the Gunpowder Plot of 1605, a nobleman who knowingly plans to kill an anointed king would be a terrifying figure, and Shakespeare’s emphasis on choice makes Macbeth fully responsible.

Ambition is also shared, and Lady Macbeth shows its unnatural cost. Macbeth’s letter calls her ‘my dearest partner of greatness’, and she immediately fears that his nature is ‘too full o’ th’ milk of human kindness’. To make herself capable of murder she calls on spirits to ‘unsex me here’, rejecting the nurturing role a Jacobean audience expected of women. Yet her ambition cannot overcome nature: she cannot kill Duncan because he ‘resembled / My father as he slept’, and by Act 3 she admits ‘Nought’s had, all’s spent’. Her final appearance, sleepwalking and scrubbing at a ‘damned spot’, shows ambition reduced to guilt. Shakespeare therefore suggests that ambition which defies the natural order of family, gender and conscience is ultimately self-destructive.

Once achieved, ambition becomes fear. As king, Macbeth complains that ‘To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus’, and his resentment of a ‘fruitless crown’ and ‘barren sceptre’ drives him to murder Banquo, whose descendants the Witches promised would be kings. Here context sharpens the meaning: King James claimed descent from Banquo, so the play flatters the king by showing Banquo’s line as the legitimate future while Macbeth’s ambition is sterile. Macbeth’s violence escalates until, in Act 4, he decides that ‘The very firstlings of my heart shall be / The firstlings of my hand’, and he orders the slaughter of Macduff’s ‘wife, his babes’. Ambition has turned a hesitant, conscience-stricken soldier into a tyrant who acts without thought.

Finally, Shakespeare shows that ambition leads to emptiness. In the ‘Tomorrow’ soliloquy, Macbeth describes life as ‘a tale / Told by an idiot, full of sound and fury, / Signifying nothing’. The crown he murdered for has given him no meaning, only a sense that time ‘Creeps in this petty pace’. Yet he still fights, crying ‘Lay on, Macduff’, a last glimpse of the courage that made him great. The play ends with Malcolm, a king who in Act 4 listed the ‘king-becoming graces’, promising to restore order ‘by the grace of Grace’. Shakespeare’s structure thus moves from disorder to divine order, confirming that the rightful king rules by God’s will, while individual ambition, however brilliant, ends in ‘nothing’.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents ambition not as a destiny forced on Macbeth by the Witches but as a desire he chooses to feed, and by tracing it from ‘vaulting ambition’ to ‘nothing’ he warns a Jacobean audience that any ambition which overturns God’s chosen order destroys the person who pursues it.
why: **AO1**: a conceptual thesis (choice; emptiness; purpose) sustained across the whole play, with well-chosen short quotations from all five acts.
**AO3**: Gunpowder Plot, divine right, gender expectations, King James and Banquo, all used to explain meaning.
Range: Macbeth, Lady Macbeth, Banquo, Malcolm.
Ends with a judgement that links structure, context and theme.
